Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Structural Basis for Cytoplasmic Dynein-1 Regulation by Lis1" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Anna Akhmanova as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Xin Xiang (Reviewer #1); Deanna Smith (Reviewer #2); Gira Bhabha (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another and agreed that this first high resolution structure of a Lis1 bound to dynein is an important piece of work. The Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) The reviewers agreed that your model for the role of Lis1 in controlling affinity for microtubules and determining plus end localization needs more discussion of other papers in the field. Please see reviewer 1 for details.

2) If possible the reviewers ask you to conduct some experiments at high salt under conditions where Lis1 is reported to affect yeast dynein processivity. Please see reviewer 1 for details.

3) The reviewers had some difficulty following the species of LIS1 and dynein, the specific constructs, and the mutations used for each experiment (and also to some extent in the discussion) – can you try to standardize names of constructs and proteins. For example: Reviewer 2 main point, Reviewer 1 point 8, Reviewer 3 point 1, Reviewer 1 point 5.

More detailed questions and suggestions from the reviewers can be found in the full reviews below.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

In this manuscript, the authors reported the first high-resolution (3.1Å) structure of the dynein-Lis1 complex using yeast proteins including the dynein motor domain and LIS1 dimer. This high-resolution structure allows the authors to reveal new details of interaction interfaces, specifically the LIS1-binding site on AAA5, the LIS1-binding site on the stalk as well as the contact site between the two LIS1 propellers (one binds the ring and the other binds stalk). The authors made specific mutations (in LIS1 or dynein) to investigate the significance of these interactions. The functional study was done by using both in vitro (binding curve and effect on in vitro velocity) and in vivo assays (nuclear positioning and dynein localization in yeast). Finally, they also made mutations in human dynein that affect LIS1 binding to the same sites (ring and stalk) and investigated the functional significance of the involved amino acids in cargo-adapter- and dynactin-mediated dynein activation/motility assay. Their results suggest that these sites are important for the formation of active human dynein complexes. Overall, the authors have done a very impressive and beautiful series of experiments. The potential impact of such a high-resolution structure is obvious and their functional analysis has also generated great insights. The data are in general of high quality and nicely presented, and the paper is very well written. However, their model is problematic. It is mainly based on the idea that LIS1 enhances the dynein-microtubule interaction to keep dynein at the microtubule plus end (they think that this tight microtubule binding at the plus end would in turn enhance the formation of the active complex containing dynein, dynactin and cargo adapters). This idea is not consistent with published data (see my point #1 below). Thus, the model figure as well as some discussion points will need to be revised or replaced accordingly. In addition, in vitro assays were done to test whether the mutations affect Pac1/LIS1's ability to induce a tight dynein-microtubule binding or an inhibition of dynein motility, while Marzo, et al., 2020 NCB showed co-migration of dynein and Pac1/LIS1 as well as Pac1/LIS1's ability in enhancing dynein processivity if salt concentration is increased for the in vitro motility assay. I wonder if the authors could try to use higher salt concentrations in the in vitro motility assay, which seems worthwhile because the enhancement of dynein processivity has been linked to the ability of LIS1 in promoting the open state of dynein (the current LIS1-mechanism model that the authors also emphasized in the Discussion). Below I provide more detailed comments for the authors to consider during the revision.

1. Currently, the model emphasized the idea that the LIS1-enhanced dynein-microtubule interaction enhances the microtubule-plus-end accumulation of dynein, which in turn promotes active complex formation. This is inconsistent with experimental findings: In the budding yeast, the microtubule-binding domain is not required for the plus-end accumulation of dynein (Lammers and Markus 2015). In mammalian cells (as well as filamentous fungi), dynactin is needed for the plus-end accumulation of dynein (Xiang et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2003, 2008, Lenz et al., 2006; Egan et al., 2012, Splinter et al., 2012., Yao et al., 2012) and this is also true in vitro in reconstituted systems (Duellburg et al., 2014; Baumbach et al., 2017; Jha et al., 2017). Would it be better to have a model figure summarizing the current findings on the separation-of-function mutants?

2. It would be better to mention in the Introduction section that LIS1 has recently been implicated in preventing dynein from adopting the autoinhibited phi structure when you mentioned its role in complex formation.

3. Data were presented to argue for an inconsistency with a "tethering" model in which LIS1 tethers dynein to microtubules non-specifically. This was done to argue against the idea proposed by Marzo et al., 2020 that the Pac1/LIS1-caused speed reduction of dynein is due to the non-specific binding of Pac1/LIS1 to microtubules. However, Marzo et al. showed that Pac1/LIS1 does not need to bind dynein to cause a speed reduction, since dynein complexed with Pac1 or not complexed with Pac1 gets the same kind of speed reduction. This point will need to be considered. In addition, since the LIS15A mutant binds to neither dynein nor microtubules, do you have any previous data suggesting that the mutant protein is folded properly or at least expressed well in vivo? This would help strengthen the argument that these amino acids bind microtubules directly. Also, the dimeric LIS1 (LIS1 WT) does seem to lower the velocity more dramatically (Figure 3C), and this also needs to be considered because the argument that dynein-binding and microtubule-binding cannot possibly use the same site of LIS1 only works when a monomer is considered. Given these problems, and the fact that there is no good model explaining how LIS1 affects the mechanochemistry of dynein (aside from phi opening), it may be easier not to put too much effort into this argument but just focus on the new structural data.

4. The interaction between the two LIS1 propellers is important, which is a significant result. Since Htet et al., 2020 NCB showed that LIS1 monomer is effective in promoting active complex formation in vitro, it seems that monomers at a high concentration can still lead to propeller interaction, and you may want to mention this point in this context. Also, it would be nice to cite an early Aspergillus paper showing that LIS1 dimerization is important in vivo (Ahn and Morris 2001 JBC).

5. In Figure 2 G and other figures where you checked LIS1's ability to lower dynein's affinity for microtubules in the presence of ATP-Vi, did you use wild type or the wB-AAA3 mutant?

6. Figure 6, it is unclear where the cortical dynein dots are. It would be better to show a merge with the bright-field images to show cortical dynein or at least use arrows or circles to mark the positions of the signals in all images. Also, would it be better to show representative images of the new mutants rather than just lis1∆?

7. It would be better to at least briefly mention in the main text how you quantify dynein for the binding curves.

8. The dynein mutant defective in binding AAA5 does show a little lowered level, and the authors can state something like "a slightly reduced expression level was observed". Please include a simple sequence alignment figure to show the positions of the mutated amino acids or those in the contacting sites in human dynein and yeast dynein heavy chains.

9. Lis1S248Q and Lis1F185D, I189D, R494A are capable of inducing tight microtubule binding in the presence of ATP but mutants carrying these mutations show a clear nuclear-positioning phenotype in yeast. This at least argues against the tight MT-binding being the only key effect of LIS1 in vivo. What would be the other key effects? "The weakening of dynein's interactions with microtubules when AAA3 is bound to ATP" does not seem to agree with the genetic data from Aspergillus that the wB-AAA3 mutation allows the LIS1 function to be bypassed. It seems more likely that LIS1's effect on promoting the open dynein state is relevant in vivo as this was shown in both yeast and Aspergillus. For these two mutants, I wonder if the open dynein (phi mutant) would suppress their nuclear-positioning defect. If so, that would be very interesting. Although I don't think these experiments are absolutely needed for the publication of this work, it would indeed be better to at least discuss these individual mutants in light of this current model of LIS1 action (i.e. overcoming the phi state and promoting the open state).

10. LIS1 seems to be requited for both the plus-end accumulation and the cortical interaction of dynein, but the beauty of the Lis1S248Q mutation is that it seems to only affect the dynein-dynactin-Num1 complex formation. You should discuss this. Could the nuclear-positioning defect of this mutant be suppressed by the phi mutation or by the AAA3 Walker B mutation? Would this mutation prevent dynein from leaving the microtubule plus end when the Num1 CC domains are overexpressed (Lammers and Markus 2015)? These experiments were doable in Aspergillus only because LIS1 is not required for the plus-end dynein accumulation, but now you have gotten this wonderful function-separating mutant that can be used in yeast for various future assays!

11. "….reach the cell cortex, the site where active yeast dynein-dynactin complexes interact with the candidate activating adaptor, Num1 (Figure 8A, panel iii) (Heil-Chapdelaine et al., 2000; Lammers and Markus, 2015; Lee et al., 2003; Sheeman et al..)". It is better to add Tang et al. 2012 JCB after this statement because this paper dissected the dynein-cortex interaction in detail. Also, it's better not to call the dynein-dynactin complexes "active" because it is only active after Num1 binding (Lammers and Markus 2015).

12. The structure was solved using the yeast dynein motor domain containing a Walker B mutation in AAA3 (E2488Q). Given the recent genetic data from Aspergillus that the wB-AAA3 mutation bypasses the requirement of LIS1 (Qiu et al., 2021, bioRxiv), some people may think that the newly identified interactions are not important in other systems. Thus, it would be better to mention that the human dynein used for structural work (Htet et al., 2020 NCB) is a wild type with linkers bent, but LIS1 binding at the stalk was still revealed, suggesting that these interactions sites play roles in multiple dynein states.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

It was difficult to keep track of dynein and LIS1 constructs used in the study. It might be better to use PAC1 for experiments with the yeast protein and LIS1 in experiments with human protein. Also, the simple term "dynein" should probably be reserved for the holoenzyme and descriptors used to indicate when other forms of dynein are used (monomeric, mutant etc).

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

We enjoyed reading this manuscript, which was very well written and presented. We have a few comments below that we ask the authors to address.

1) We had a hard time figuring out what dynein construct was used for the cryo EM structure. Could the authors make this clear in the methods/table please?

2) As the authors note, nucleotide density is somewhat ambiguous. We noted that this may be the case for AAA4 as well. If it was not attempted already, we suggest signal subtraction, re-centering and local refinement perhaps focused on AAA2-3-4, AAA5-6-1L, AAA6-1-2 and around the two Lis1 binding sites. The resolution of this structure is already very impressive and the field would benefit from the highest resolution dynein-Lis1 structure possible; signal subtraction / local refinement may provide additional resolution which could allow to unambiguously assign nucleotide density and some parts of the interface.

3) Line 262 – the authors mention that "Arg 494 was also mutated to Ala to remove the only hydrogen bond donor/acceptor in the interface". However, it seems that D183 and K178 may form a salt bridge between the two Lis1 b-propellers and contribute to the interface?

4) It seems that R3476 (dynein) and E253 (Lis1) could interact if the E253 rotamer was changed, and indeed these residues were chosen to mutate. Since there is not density defining this rotamer, do the authors think that switching the rotamer to facilitate salt bridging would make sense? Currently R3476 looks like it interacts with D3487, so it's possible it can switch between these two interactions.

5) In the structure statistics table (Supplementary file 2) please include: cc values, sphericity value from 3D FSC

6) Great use of the streptavidin affinity grids for a really tough sample!

7) Throughout the manuscript, it may be useful to name the Lis1 chains in some way so it is easy to follow which b-propeller if being referenced at each instance

8) Figure 6: We found the microscopy assay a bit hard to follow, and would appreciate if it were made a bit more clear. A few things we were unsure of:

– Are the measurements being made in the 20% of cells that are the aberrant binucleate cells?

– Was this all done by live cell imaging? Or were cells fixed and analysed?

– Because of the background, the images in Figure 6C are hard to follow. We were wondering if zooming in further may help. A cortical marker or + end marker would also be helpful but may not be necessary. Maybe the authors could draw an outline of the cells to help the readers to see better, which would be an easy fix.

9) Figure 1E-H is a bit hard to follow with the density and the models. We suggest to highlight interactions using just the models, and show the map quality in the supplement.

10) Figure 2E – do the authors find it surprising that the affinity is not changed more? We would have expected to see more of a change in binding affinities.

11) For the mutants that were made, is it clear that they all fold properly/are stable?

12) Could the authors include statistical analysis for Figure 2C,D, Figure 4B and 5B, to test significance as they have done for other assays?

claims.claim: Lis1's role in forming active complexes is conserved and required for in vivo function in S. cerevisiae and A. nidulans.
claims.source: Studies in S. cerevisiae and the filamentous fungus Aspergillus nidulans suggest that this role for Lis1 in forming active complexes is conserved and required for in vivo function (Marzo et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claims.claim: The presence of Lis1 causes dynein to bind microtubules more tightly under some nucleotide conditions.
claims.source: One common theme in these studies was that the presence of Lis1 causes dynein to bind microtubules more tightly under some nucleotide conditions (DeSantis et al., 2017; Htet et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2012; McKenney et al., 2010; Yamada et al., 2008), which in the context of a moving molecule correlates with decreased velocity (DeSantis et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2012; Yamada et al., 2008) or an increased ability of dynein to remain bound to microtubules under load (McKenney et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claims.claim: In yeast, Lis1 induces a weak microtubule binding state in dynein when the nucleotide bound at AAA3 is ATP or an ATP mimic.
claims.source: In yeast, the nucleotide state of dynein's AAA3 domain seems to regulate this as Lis1 (called Pac1 in yeast, referred to as 'Lis1' here) induces a weak microtubule binding state in dynein when the nucleotide bound at AAA3 is ATP or an ATP mimic (DeSantis et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claims.claim: Different modes of dynein regulation by yeast Lis1 correlate with the number of Lis1 ß-propellers observed interacting with dynein by cryo-EM.
claims.source: These different modes of dynein regulation by yeast Lis1 correlate with the number of Lis1 ß-propellers observed interacting with dynein by cryo-EM, with a single ß-propeller bound to dynein at sitering in the absence of nucleotide at AAA3, and two ß-propellers bound to dynein at sitering and sitestalk when the nucleotide at AAA3 is ATP or an ATP mimic (DeSantis et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claims.claim: Mutations that link nucleotide hydrolysis at AAA3 to Lis1 have been reported genetically.
claims.source: Genetically, mutations that link nucleotide hydrolysis at AAA3 to Lis1 have also been reported (Qiu et al., 2021; Willins et al., 1997; Zhuang et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claims.claim: The dyneinE2488Q–(Lis1)2 complex structure was determined to a nominal resolution of 3.1 Å.
claims.source: This approach allowed us to determine the structure of yeast dyneinE2448Q bound to wild-type yeast Lis1 in the presence of ATP vanadate to a nominal resolution of 3.1 Å (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryo-EM data in the figures.

claims.claim: In the dyneinE2488Q–(Lis1)2 structure, dynein's AAA ring is 'closed'.
claims.source: In our structure, dyneinE2488Q's AAA ring is 'closed,' which is seen when dynein's microtubule binding domain is in its low-affinity state, the linker is bent (Bhabha et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2015), and when two Lis1 ß-propellers interact with dynein (DeSantis et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The two Lis1 ß-propellers in the structure likely come from the same homodimer.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the cryo-EM data processing.

claims.claim: Binding of Lis1 at sitering primarily involves the smaller face of the ß-propeller in Lis1 and an alpha helix in AAA4 of dynein.
claims.source: Binding of Lis1 at sitering primarily involves the smaller face of the ß-propeller in Lis1 and an alpha helix in AAA4 of dyneinE2488Q (Figures 1E and 2A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in the figures.

claims.claim: There is an additional interaction between dynein and Lis1 at sitering that involves a contact with a loop in AAA5.
claims.source: Our high-resolution structure also allowed us to unambiguously map an additional interaction between dyneinE2488Q and Lis1 at sitering that involves a contact with a loop in AAA5 (Figures 1E and 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in the figures.

claims.claim: Lis1 binds to dynein at sitestalk using its side and makes interactions with coiled-coil 1 (CC1) of dynein's stalk.
claims.source: Lis1 binds to dynein at sitestalk using its side and makes interactions with coiled-coil 1 (CC1) of dynein's stalk, as well as a previously unknown contact with a loop in AAA4 (residues 2935–2942) (Figures 1F and 2A, B and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in the figures.

claims.claim: There is a previously unknown contact between Lis1 at sitestalk and a loop in AAA4 (residues 2935–2942).
claims.source: Lis1 binds to dynein at sitestalk using its side and makes interactions with coiled-coil 1 (CC1) of dynein's stalk, as well as a previously unknown contact with a loop in AAA4 (residues 2935–2942) (Figures 1F and 2A, B and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in the figures.

claims.claim: The Lis1s bound at sitering and sitestalk directly interact with each other.
claims.source: As suggested by the continuous density in our previous low-resolution structure (DeSantis et al., 2017), the Lis1s bound at sitering and sitestalk directly interact with each other (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, Figure 2A, B and E, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in the figures.

claims.claim: The ATP binding sites at AAA1, AAA2, AAA3, and AAA4 are all occupied by nucleotides in the structure.

claims.claim: ADP is bound at AAA4 in the structure.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claims.claim: The authors were unable to resolve whether ATP or ADP-vanadate was bound at AAA1-AAA3 and chose to model ATP into each binding pocket.

claims.claim: All the interactions involving Lis1 are maintained in the different conformations observed in 3D variability analysis.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the 3D variability analysis.

claims.claim: Lis1E253A, H254A and dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 both exhibit a binucleate phenotype equivalent to that seen with deletion of Lis1 or dynein.
claims.source: We found that Lis1E253A, H254A and dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 both exhibit a binucleate phenotype that is equivalent to that seen with deletion of Lis1 or dynein (Figure 3B–D), suggesting that the interaction between Lis1 and dynein at AAA5 is required for yeast Lis1's ability to regulate dynein in vivo.

claims.claim: The interaction between Lis1 and dynein at AAA5 is required for yeast Lis1's ability to regulate dynein in vivo.
claims.source: We found that Lis1E253A, H254A and dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 both exhibit a binucleate phenotype that is equivalent to that seen with deletion of Lis1 or dynein (Figure 3B–D), suggesting that the interaction between Lis1 and dynein at AAA5 is required for yeast Lis1's ability to regulate dynein in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the in vivo data.

claims.claim: Mutations at the Lis1–AAA5 interface led to an ~1.75-fold decrease in the affinity of Lis1 for dynein.
claims.source: We found that mutations at the Lis1–AAA5 interface, either on Lis1 (Lis1E253A, H254A) or on dynein (dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476), led to an ~1.75-fold decrease in the affinity of Lis1 for dynein (Figure 3E).

claims.claim: Lis1E253A, H254A decreased Lis1's ability to enhance the binding of dynein to microtubules in the presence of ATP.
claims.source: As expected for a mutation that would disrupt Lis1's interaction at sitering, we found that Lis1E253A, H254A decreased Lis1's ability to enhance the binding of dynein to microtubules in the presence of ATP (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the microtubule binding data in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Lis1E253A, H254A did not affect Lis1's ability to lower dynein's affinity for microtubules in the presence of ATP-Vi.
claims.source: In contrast, Lis1E253A, H254A did not affect Lis1's ability to lower dynein's affinity for microtubules in the presence of ATP-Vi (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the microtubule binding data in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: In the absence of Lis1, dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 had a similar velocity to wild-type dynein.
claims.source: Here, we found that in the absence of Lis1, dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 had a similar velocity to wild-type dynein, indicating that the mutation does not affect the motile properties of the motor (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the single-molecule motility data in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Lis1 was less effective at slowing the velocity of dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 compared to wild-type dynein.
claims.source: In contrast, Lis1 was less effective at slowing the velocity of dyneinΔN3475, ΔR3476 compared to wild-type dynein.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the single-molecule motility data in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: The interaction of yeast Lis1 with dynein at AAA5 contributes to Lis1's regulation of dynein at sitering.
claims.source: Thus, the interaction of yeast Lis1 with dynein at AAA5 contributes to Lis1's regulation of dynein at sitering.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Yeast cells expressing Lis1S248Q showed a defect in nuclear segregation.

claims.claim: The new contact at sitestalk between AAA4 of dynein and Lis1 is required for Lis1's ability to regulate dynein in vivo.

claims.claim: Lis1S248Q showed a moderate decrease in binding affinity for dynein monomers.

claims.claim: Lis1S248Q failed to decrease microtubule binding in the presence of ATP-Vi.

claims.claim: Lis1S248Q is the first Lis1 mutant capable of specifically targeting regulation at sitestalk.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the characterization of Lis1S248Q.

claims.claim: Lis1F185D, I189D, R494A resulted in a binucleate yeast cell phenotype comparable to that seen with deletion of Lis1.

claims.claim: The interaction between Lis1 β-propellers is required for Lis1's ability to regulate dynein in vivo.

claims.claim: Lis1F185D, I189D, R494A has an affinity for dynein comparable to that of wild-type Lis1.
claims.source: In vitro, Lis1F185D, I189D, R494A has an affinity for dynein comparable to that of wild-type Lis1 (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: Lis1F185D, I189D, R494A not only lost its ability to decrease dynein's affinity for microtubules in the presence of ATP-Vi, it increased it.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the microtubule binding data in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Regulation of dynein at sitestalk requires both binding at sitestalk and the interaction between Lis1's ß-propellers.

claims.claim: While sitering is very similar in both open-ring and closed-ring dynein structures, sitestalk has shifted ~3 Å and rotated 20° away from where Lis1stalk would be located in the open-ring structure.
claims.source: A comparison of our structure of dyneinE2488Q –(Lis1)2 (with dynein's ring in its closed conformation) with that of yeast dynein in an open-ring conformation (PDB: 4AKI; Schmidt et al., 2012) showed that while sitering is very similar in both structures, sitestalk has shifted ~3 Å and rotated 20° away from where Lis1stalk would be located (Figure 5F).

claims.claim: The interaction between the two Lis1 ß-propellers prevents Lis1 from binding to dynein at sitestalk when dynein is in its open-ring state.
claims.source: This suggests that the interaction between the two Lis1 ß-propellers prevents Lis1 from binding to dynein at sitestalk when dynein is in its open-ring state (high affinity for the microtubule), as we had hypothesized previously (DeSantis et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the structural comparison.

claims.claim: Deletion of Lis1 causes a significant decrease in dynein foci at SPBs, microtubule plus ends, and the cell cortex.

claims.claim: Mutation of sitering (Lis1E253A, H254A) showed a significant decrease in dynein foci at SPBs, microtubule plus ends, and the cell cortex.

claims.claim: Lis1S248Q is a separation-of-function mutant that could be a useful tool to further understand the mechanism of dynein regulation by Lis1.

claims.claim: sitering, sitestalk and the Lis1–Lis1 interface are important for localizing dynein to the cell cortex.

results.result: The authors determined the first high-resolution (3.1 Å) cryo-EM structure of the yeast dynein–Lis1 complex, revealing molecular details of dynein-Lis1 contacts at sitering and sitestalk, contacts between Lis1 β-propellers, and nucleotide occupancy at AAA domains. The structure was achieved using streptavidin affinity grids to overcome preferred orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C51 and C90-C91 collectively describe the structural determination and analysis. The 3.1 Å resolution is supported by cryo-EM data (Figures 1, 2, supplementary figures), FSC curves, and detailed methods. The structure reveals previously unknown contacts at AAA5 (sitering) and AAA4 (sitestalk), nucleotide occupancy, and Lis1-Lis1 interfaces. Use of streptavidin affinity grids is documented in methods and cited appropriately.

results.result: Structure-guided mutations disrupting the Lis1-AAA5 interaction (Lis1E253A,H254A and dyneinΔN3475,ΔR3476) cause binucleate phenotypes in yeast equivalent to Lis1 deletion, reduce Lis1-dynein binding affinity ~1.75-fold, impair Lis1's ability to enhance dynein-microtubule binding in ATP, and reduce Lis1's effect on dynein velocity, demonstrating that the AAA5 contact contributes to Lis1 regulation at sitering.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C59 are supported by multiple complementary assays: in vivo nuclear segregation (Figure 3B-D), binding affinity measurements (Figure 3E), microtubule binding assays (Figure 3F-G), and single-molecule velocity measurements (Figure 3H). Statistical analyses are provided with appropriate replicates (n=3-6). The mutations are structure-guided and expressed at wild-type levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

results.result: The Lis1S248Q mutation, targeting a newly identified contact between Lis1 and AAA4 at sitestalk, causes nuclear segregation defects in yeast, moderately reduces Lis1-dynein binding, maintains regulation at sitering (ATP-induced tight microtubule binding) but abolishes regulation at sitestalk (ATP-Vi-induced weak microtubule binding), representing the first separation-of-function mutant specific for sitestalk.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by nuclear segregation assays (Figure 4B), binding measurements (Figure 4C), and nucleotide-specific microtubule binding assays (Figure 4D-E). The separation-of-function phenotype is clearly demonstrated: the mutant retains sitering function but loses sitestalk function. Expression at wild-type levels is confirmed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Statistical analyses with appropriate replicates are provided.

results.result: Mutations disrupting the Lis1-Lis1 interface (Lis1F185D,I189D,R494A) cause binucleate phenotypes equivalent to Lis1 deletion, maintain wild-type binding affinity and sitering regulation, but lose sitestalk regulation and paradoxically increase microtubule binding in ATP-Vi. Structural comparison shows sitestalk shifts ~3 Å and rotates 20° between open and closed dynein ring conformations, suggesting the Lis1-Lis1 interface prevents Lis1 binding at sitestalk when dynein is in its open-ring (high microtubule affinity) state.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 are supported by nuclear segregation assays (Figure 5B), binding measurements (Figure 5C), microtubule binding assays (Figure 5D-E), and structural comparisons (Figure 5F). The data demonstrate that both sitestalk binding and the Lis1-Lis1 interface are required for proper sitestalk regulation. The structural comparison with PDB 4AKI provides mechanistic insight. Statistical analyses with appropriate replicates are provided.

results.result: Analysis of dynein localization in yeast cells shows that sitering mutations (Lis1E253A,H254A) cause defects equivalent to Lis1 deletion at all three sites (SPBs, microtubule plus ends, cortex), while sitestalk (Lis1S248Q) and Lis1-Lis1 interface (Lis1F185D,I189D,R494A) mutations show intermediate phenotypes at SPBs and cortex. Notably, Lis1S248Q is the only mutant with no defect in dynein localization to microtubule plus ends, confirming it as a separation-of-function mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 are supported by live-cell imaging with quantification of dynein foci at three distinct cellular locations (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Statistical analyses using Kruskal-Wallis tests with n=120 cells per condition are provided. The separation-of-function phenotype of Lis1S248Q is clearly demonstrated by its unique retention of plus-end localization function.

results.result: A Phi-disrupting dynein mutation (dyneinD2868K) rescues the binucleate phenotype caused by the sitering Lis1 mutation (Lis1E253A,H254A), but when combined with this Lis1 mutation, dynein cortical localization is reduced compared to dyneinD2868K alone. This suggests Lis1 binding at sitering has an additional role in dynein regulation beyond relieving autoinhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83, C97, C102-C103 are supported by nuclear segregation assays (Figure 7A) and cortical localization quantification (Figure 7B-C) with appropriate statistical analyses (n=4 replicates for nuclear segregation, n=120 cells for localization). The genetic epistasis experiment is well-designed and the interpretation is appropriately cautious, noting that more sensitive assays in other organisms show incomplete rescue (C98).

results.result: Mutations in human dynein at both sitering (K2898A,E2902G,E2903S,E2904G) and sitestalk (E3196A,Q3198A,N3202A) reduce Lis1 binding affinity ~3-fold, do not affect basal dynein-dynactin-Hook3 complex velocity or processivity, but significantly impair Lis1's ability to increase velocity and processivity of these complexes, demonstrating that sitering and sitestalk contacts are important for Lis1's role in forming activated human dynein complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 and C11 are supported by binding measurements (Figure 8B), single-molecule motility assays with dynein-dynactin-Hook3 complexes (Figure 8C-D), and similar results with BicD2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A). Statistical analyses with appropriate replicates (n=3 for binding, ≥150 events for motility) are provided. The mutations do not affect basal dynein function, supporting specificity for Lis1-mediated regulation.

results.result: The structure shows that Lis1 binding at sitering is sterically incompatible with dynein's autoinhibited Phi conformation. The authors propose a model where cytosolic dynein exists in Phi conformation, while dynein in kinesin transport complexes or at microtubule plus ends (both containing Lis1) is no longer autoinhibited, with Lis1 binding shifting the equilibrium from Phi to open conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 and C122 represent a mechanistic model based on structural inference (C92 supported by comparison with Zhang et al., 2017) and prior literature (C95-C96 cited). However, the model (C93-C94, C122) is explicitly presented as a proposal/hypothesis in the Discussion without direct experimental validation in this manuscript. While the steric incompatibility is structurally supported, the proposed conformational states at different cellular locations are speculative.

results.result: The authors discuss evidence suggesting Lis1 may have additional roles beyond disrupting Phi autoinhibition: (1) Phi-disrupting dynein mutants do not completely rescue Lis1 mutations in sensitive assays in Aspergillus and yeast, (2) Phi-disrupting mutants do not completely abolish Lis1 requirement for human complex formation in vitro, and (3) their data suggest a role for microtubule binding in dynein reaching the cortex. They propose that dynein complex assembly likely involves multiple steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101, C105-C106 are appropriately supported by citations to prior work (C98-C100) and the authors' own data (C102-C103, C105). The interpretation is cautious and acknowledges uncertainty. The claims represent synthesis of multiple lines of evidence rather than definitive conclusions, which is appropriate for Discussion content. The suggestion of additional Lis1 roles is well-justified by the incomplete rescue phenotypes.

results.result: The introduction establishes the biological context: LIS1 mutations cause lissencephaly in humans; Lis1 is conserved and regulates cytoplasmic dynein-1; dynein is a major microtubule motor with diverse cellular functions; dynein exists in autoinhibited Phi conformation and requires dynactin, activating adaptors, and Lis1 for full activity; Lis1 is a dimeric β-propeller protein that binds dynein at two sites (sitering and sitestalk) and affects dynein's mechanochemistry and complex formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C39, C108-C110 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited throughout the introduction. These claims provide context for the current work and are supported by extensive literature citations. The claims are not novel findings of this manuscript but rather necessary background. All statements are appropriately attributed to prior work.

results.result: The manuscript cites prior work from the authors' lab and others establishing: tight microtubule binding by dynein in ATP is mediated by sitering while weak binding in ATP-Vi requires both sites; Lis1 slows yeast dynein velocity; yeast dynein moves processively without cofactors; yeast dynein is active at the cortex and reaches it via kinesin transport or cytosolic recruitment; Lis1 is required for dynein localization to SPBs, plus ends, and cortex; and Lis1 is important for forming activated complexes with various adaptors including TRAK2 and Hook2.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C119, C123-C124 represent prior work appropriately cited in Results and Discussion sections. These claims provide context for interpreting the current findings and are supported by citations to published literature, including the authors' previous work. The claims are not novel findings but necessary background for understanding the experimental design and interpretation.

results.result: The Discussion concludes that: dynein's microtubule binding domain is not required to reach the cortex (cited); Lis1's role in complex assembly will likely be required for other activating adaptors (inference); the importance of sitering and sitestalk in both human and yeast supports conserved Lis1 regulation; and the field is coalescing around a unified model for Lis1 regulation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C104, C120-C121, C107 represent appropriate synthesis and interpretation in the Discussion. C104 is cited to prior work; C120 is a reasonable inference from the data on TRAK2, Hook2, Ninl, and BicDL1; C121 is directly supported by the manuscript's findings in both yeast and human systems; C107 is appropriately supported by extensive citations to recent convergent findings in the field.

results.result: The abstract claims that structure-guided mutations show the dynein-Lis1 contacts are required to regulate yeast dynein's mechanochemistry and in vivo function.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are high-level summary statements in the abstract that are supported by the detailed experimental results in Figures 3-7, including mechanochemistry assays (microtubule binding, velocity measurements) and in vivo assays (nuclear segregation, localization). These abstract claims accurately summarize the major findings of the manuscript.
